title: Hyades (star cluster)
description: Open cluster in the constellation Taurus
wiki_lead:
The Hyades (; Greek: Ὑάδες; also known as Caldwell 41, Collinder 50, or Melotte 25) is the nearest open cluster and one of the best-studied star clusters. Located about 153 light-years (47 parsecs) away from the Sun, it consists of a roughly spherical group of hundreds of stars sharing the same age, place of origin, chemical characteristics, and motion through space.
From the perspective of observers on Earth, the Hyades Cluster appears in the constellation Taurus, where its brightest stars form a "V" shape along with the still-brighter Aldebaran. However, Aldebaran is unrelated to the Hyades, as it is located much closer to Earth (65 light-years) and merely happens to lie along the same line of sight. The moving group CWNU 1242 also shares the line of sight to the Hyades, but is likewise not associated with the Hyades, being 949 light-years away.
The five brightest member stars of the Hyades have consumed the hydrogen fuel at their cores and have evolved into giant stars. Together with Aldebaran, four of these stars, Gamma, Delta1, Epsilon, and Theta2 Tauri, form an asterism that is traditionally identified as the head of Taurus the Bull. The fifth of the giants is Theta1 Tauri, a tight naked-eye companion to the brighter Theta2 Tauri. Epsilon Tauri, known as Ain (the "Bull's Eye"), has a gas giant exoplanet candidate, the first planet to be found in any open cluster.
The age of the Hyades is estimated to be about 625 million years. The core of the cluster, where stars are the most densely packed, has a radius of 8.8 light-years (2.7 parsecs), and the cluster's tidal radius – where the stars become more strongly influenced by the gravity of the surrounding Milky Way galaxy – is 33 light-years (10 parsecs). However, about one-third of confirmed member stars have been observed well outside the latter boundary, in the cluster's extended halo; these stars are probably in the process of escaping from its gravitational influence.

Location and motion
The cluster is sufficiently close to the Sun that its distance can be directly measured by observing the amount of parallax shift of the member stars as the Earth orbits the Sun. This measurement has been performed with great accuracy using the Hipparcos satellite and the Hubble Space Telescope. An alternative method of computing the distance is to fit the cluster members to a standardized infrared color–magnitude diagram for stars of their type, and use the resulting data to infer their intrinsic brightness. Comparing this data to the brightness of the stars as seen from Earth allows their distances to be estimated. Both methods have yielded a distance estimate of 153 light-years (47 parsecs) to the cluster center. The fact that these independent measurements agree makes the Hyades an important rung on the cosmic distance ladder method for estimating the distances of extragalactic objects.
The stars of the Hyades are more enriched in heavier elements than the Sun and other ordinary stars in the solar neighborhood, with the overall cluster metallicity measured at +0.14. The Hyades Cluster is related to other stellar groups in the Sun's vicinity. Its age, metallicity, and proper motion coincide with those of the larger and more distant Praesepe Cluster, and the trajectories of both clusters can be traced back to the same region of space, indicating a common origin. Another associate is the Hyades Stream, a large collection of scattered stars that also share a similar trajectory with the Hyades Cluster. Recent results have found that at least 15% of stars in the Hyades Stream share the same chemical fingerprint as the Hyades cluster stars. However, about 85% of stars in the Hyades Stream have been shown to be completely unrelated to the original cluster on the grounds of dissimilar age and metallicity; their common motion is attributed to tidal effects of the massive rotating bar at the center of the Milky Way galaxy. grok_lead: The Hyades is an open star cluster in the constellation Taurus, situated approximately 153 light-years from the Sun and recognized as the nearest such cluster to Earth. It comprises around 600 bona fide member stars that originated from the same molecular cloud, sharing common proper motion and chemical composition, with an age of approximately 700 million years. The cluster appears as a distinctive V-shaped asterism to the naked eye, outlining the face of the bull in Taurus and easily located by extending a line from Orion's Belt toward the northwest. Spanning an apparent size of 330 arcminutesâlarger than the full Moon âit has an integrated visual magnitude of 0.5, making it one of the most prominent deep-sky objects visible without optical aid from mid-northern latitudes during winter evenings. Notably, the bright orange star Aldebaran (Alpha Tauri), at the tip of the V, is not a true member but a foreground giant located about twice as far away. Physically, the Hyades forms a roughly spherical group with a core radius of about 2.5â3.0 parsecs, exhibiting supersolar metallicity of [M/H] = +0.18 Â± 0.03 and moving coherently through space at a proper motion of around 45 mas/year. Its stellar population includes main-sequence stars ranging from A-type to low-mass M-dwarfs, with the brightest confirmed members being Î¸Â² Tauri (magnitude 3.40), Îµ Tauri (magnitude 3.53), and Î³ Tauri (magnitude 3.65). Recent observations, including those from the Gaia mission, have revealed extended tidal tails of escaping stars, highlighting the cluster's dynamical evolution within the Milky Way's gravitational field. As one of the best-studied open clusters, the Hyades serves as a benchmark for understanding stellar evolution, ages, and metallicities in the solar neighborhood, with its proximity enabling detailed analyses of planetary systems and low-mass companions among its members. It shares kinematic similarities with the more distant Praesepe cluster and continues to yield insights into cluster disruption through advanced surveys.
